item.content:encoded:
This post is an experiment in a new AI-assisted voice to blog capture mechanism.

The headline

Developers aren’t going away. But our job is.

AI can definitely write better code than me. And I’m not a very good coder — but I can write pretty much equivalent code to most folks that are out there. For the junior folks, it can definitely write better code.

What’s left is judgment

I was talking to somebody recently, and they mentioned the thing they do on pull requests now: it’s all about the architecture. Previous patterns they’ve run into that they wouldn’t want to repeat again. Proper levels of abstraction. Stuff like that.

As more senior people, we have the experience to identify that stuff and see that stuff. A more junior person wouldn’t.

Junior folks will learn these same skills. They just won’t be writing the code — they’ll be dictating to AI. AI will be writing the code, and I think that’s going to become the new norm.

The environment decides how fast you learn

It depends how AI-native the frameworks are.

In a greenfield scenario — entirely new product, move fast, deploy fast, everything around you is AI-native — the code doesn’t have to be perfect. It doesn’t have to be optimized, because it’s so easy to build now. You spit it out, pull it back, refine it, slice off pieces and optimize them more. In that environment, you learn quickly.

If you’re not in it, that’s a big challenge. You’re stuck in the middle of the old school: we gotta make this pull request, verify it in staging, make sure you put the ones before the twos, blah blah blah.

A lot of larger orgs aren’t AI-native right now. There are a lot of folks who understand that and are adopting it, and a lot who don’t yet know how — because it’s an entirely new learned skill. These people have been stitching together code for so long that stepping back to think about the product is hard to do.

A good example of what AI-native looks like is Swamp Club, by Adam Jacob. They have a very AI-native, AI-forward build environment that’s really impressive. His presentation on it is really good.

Vision is the bottleneck now

I think it’s a net positive. If you can think about the end result and what you want, and not have to worry about the implementation details, you get what we’re seeing everywhere — people building their own personal tools.

Look at r/homelab, or macOS apps. Every week there are ten people building the same exact tool over and over again. Which is amazing, and maybe a waste of resources. But at the same time: if you have the vision, you can build it.

Engineering speed versus the rest of the machine

The bottleneck was always resources. Now, in theory, the bottleneck should be tokens.

AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are AI-native. Supposedly they have anywhere from 10 to 500 agents running at any time in the background. There was a calendar going around of everything the Claude team shipped in 52 days, and it was mind-blowing — they’re putting out all of this stuff. At the same time, it wasn’t connected. It was all very disjoint. The product side wasn’t connected at all. Things were getting rolled out in engineering that had little or no documentation. It’s really hard for everything else to catch up. But I think it’s possible over time.

You have to look at the long horizon. That’s something Amazon always did really well when I was there. We’ve got the PR/FAQ — the press release and FAQ we write before building anything — and that’s our North Star for this product. Year one, we’re going to have one thing on it.

I think that frustrated a lot of companies that used AWS, especially the startups that were originally on it. But when I was there, I came to realize that enterprises don’t move that fast. One year in is nothing for an enterprise that’s been around for 50 or 100 years. And by the time we were five years into product development, AWS often had something that was actually really good.

Engineering speed versus the rest of the machine is something to consider.

Every layer gets absorbed

There’s the tension of layoffs happening at a lot of these companies. There have been places where almost all the docs teams have gotten laid off, so clearly enterprises are not finding value in those people.

I think it’s that AI can easily write docs, especially based off the code.

The part I can’t figure out yet

What does hiring look like? That’s the thing I don’t understand yet. I don’t know what the shape of it is going to look like. How much enterprise value can get created out of software these days?

And there’s the real crux: we don’t have a good way to bring juniors up today. How do we get them involved? How do we teach them these skills? How do we level them up? Sure, they can just type stuff into a prompt. But how do we actually get them to build well-designed product?

Product, not software

I’m using “product” there specifically instead of “software,” because I don’t think software matters anymore.

As a developer, I’m not totally worried that my job is going away. I just don’t know what it’s going to look like in five years.

Developers aren’t going away. But our job is.

item.title: Vibe Coding Rust CLIs
item.description:
This holiday break, I’ve been working on an arcane side project of resurrecting historical versions of my blog from 2002. As part of this, I’ve been digging around various S3 buckets for backups of old source code and mysql dumps. But doing so in the AWS console is not the most ergonomic, so I wanted to (have AI) whip up a quick terminal UI that could make it easier.

I’ve done this a couple times now, first with s3grep, and somebody suggested it might be good to document my journey so here we go!
item.content:encoded:
This holiday break, I’ve been working on an arcane side project of resurrecting historical versions of my blog from 2002. As part of this, I’ve been digging around various S3 buckets for backups of old source code and mysql dumps. But doing so in the AWS console is not the most ergonomic, so I wanted to (have AI) whip up a quick terminal UI that could make it easier.

I’ve done this a couple times now, first with s3grep, and somebody suggested it might be good to document my journey so here we go!

For reference, total development time was about 6 hours, including dinner and bedtime. Final lines of code is at 2,654, none of which was written by me.

Step 1: The Prompt

This is where it all starts of course. I try to be as specific as possible and describe the requirements.

Hey fren - I want to build a sweet little rust-based s3 explorer. It should function like a typical unix shell with the caveat that it operates against s3 buckets. When you first enter and do an ls it lists your available buckets. You can cd into a bucket and cd into prefixes in that bucket. You can cat files. And then here comes the magic sauce, you can also cd into different archives (zip, tar, tar.gz, bz, gz, etc). If possible the tool shouldn’t download the whole archive. For example, the tar archive itself can read gzip stream from stdin - we should be able to emulate this behavior in rust itself. In addition, if we do a recursive ls -R it should include files in those archives as well. Do you think we can make this? And also make it a pleast CLI experience. :)

Claude is pretty good now at entering plan mode and it automatically will ask clarifying questions. Previously you had to direct this, but not anymore. In this case it asked what we should name the project, what archive formats to prioritize, any other shell commands to implement, and if archive indexes should be cached.

But that was pretty much it - at this point, it whipped up a 250-line plan file and I just said “go for it”.

Key commits from this phase:

  • Initial revision 👋 - Claude’s first implementation from the prompt

Step 2: Iterate

Claude automatically defined the first phase as “Working shell that can navigate S3 buckets and read files”. In just a few minutes it was ready with the foundation of the CLI. It had already built a debug build, so I just ran that, browsed around, and made sure the basic cd and ls functionality worked.

The magic moment: cd into a tar archive and ls the contents, all streaming from S3

This looks great! I tested it out and it works perfectly :chefskiss: - remember to update your todos and continue with phase 2.

This back and forth iteration has been crucial to the success of my vibe-coded projects. Stopping to verify the functionality works as expected is key. The main challenge here becomes keeping track of the progress plan. Not to mention the inevitable compaction of the context that happens.

In order to manage these things, sometimes I’ll pop open a new session to solve a specific problem. For example, when Claude was done implementing phase 2 I went and tested it and found a bug. Instead of side-tracking the main thread, I opened a new claude session just for that:

I have another claude agent working on zip implementation for this prject, but when I try to cd into a zip file, I get the following error: <stack trace below>

Claude would fix the issue and I’d verify, then go back to the main prompt to continue. If I ran into a similar issue (like I did with tgz archives), I’d pop back into the bug fix session with a claude -r.

Back in the main prompt, I’d also sometimes ask for minor fixes or features before moving on.

Before we move on Phase 3, let’s make a couple small fixes. ls should be able to take parameters like a directory, subdirectory, or standard ls wildcard, e.g.: ls dir or ls dir/subdir or ls *.zip. Also if a directory has a space in it and is quoted, we should be able to cd into it. Like “cd backup/My Docs 2001/Backups” right now changes into backup/My. Also multiple ../../ should work too.

Claude is really good with Rust in making sure that the code continues to build and I feel like Rust’s great error messaging is quite beneficial to Claude being able to easily fix any issues that pop up as well. There’s less “guess and check” like what I’ve seen when it tries to build Python tooling.

Key commits from this phase:

  • v2, adds .zip support - Phase 2 archive support
  • Add support for tarchives - tar/tgz implementation
  • Fix ls/cd handling - Small fixes before Phase 3 (wildcard support, quoted paths)
  • Add a progress spinner - UX improvements
  • Fix cross-region s3 support - Bug fix in separate session

Step 3: Refinement

At some point, when I have the basic functionality I want, I’ll stop and ask Claude to review the code and identify any areas of improvement for code quality, redundancy, or maintenance. This time I took a page out of a random Reddit comment I found to “review the code with YAGNI+SOLID+DRY+KISS principles”.

One tricky thing here is that it doesn’t always do a good job of ensuring it shouldn’t clean things up. So you have to give enough guidance (and due diligence!) here to make sure that its assessment is accurate. I’ve found this is pretty hard. There was a good post from somebody that asked Claude to improve codebase quality 200 times and it was a great example of why you need a human in the loop.

Key commits from this phase:

  • optimizing - YAGNI+SOLID+DRY+KISS review
  • Apply cargo clippy fixes - Code quality improvements
  • cargo fmt - Formatting cleanup

Step 4: Managing Context

Ah the dreaded Context left until auto-compact counter. I’ve had good luck here with telling Claude to just keep a PLAN.md file up-to-date, except in the case of larger projects. I didn’t do that for this project, as I saw Claude created its own plan file, and regretted it. Once the auto-compaction happened, Claude forgot about the plan but luckily I still had a copy of it in ~/.claude/plans I could reference. I probably should have added a nice CLAUDE.md or directed it to write out the plan file locally, but alas.

I’ve also tried Steve Yegge’s Beads project for task management but I honestly haven’t had great luck with it. I think it’s largely a “me” issue though - I just haven’t been consistent with it. I’m excited for his new Gas Town project as well.

Step 5: Polish

Before I publish something, I like to have a basic README and at least a test or two. If I have something I can reference, all the better. With my s3grep tool I had manually built up the README and publishing workflow, so I just re-used that for this case.

I’d like to publish this on github…before I do I need a quick README and a publish workflow. You can model the readme after my other project ( https://github.com/dacort/s3grep/blob/main/README.md ) as well as the release workflow ( https://github.com/dacort/s3grep/blob/main/.github/workflows/release-plz.yml ).

I did the same with tests.

Hi there! I need to quickly clean up the tests for this project. cargo test fails because the methods don’t exist, so we can just remove those tests. I’d like to also create a set of basic integration test for the minimal required functionality (cd, cat, cd into archive) using localstack similar to how this test in s3grep runs ( https://github.com/dacort/s3grep/blob/main/tests/integration_s3.rs and https://github.com/dacort/s3grep/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml )

Key commits from this phase:

  • Add shell completion - Tab completion support
  • Add readme/release details - README modeled after s3grep
  • Add basic integration tests - Testing with localstack

Tracking Changes

I should note that after every verification step that I manually perform, I git add all the new files. I could have Claude do this I suppose, but I like the process of verifying and seeing what’s changed to at least understand the code a tiny bit.

Ship It 🚀

This is still largely manual - I create the repo myself, set up any necessary API secrets and git push when ready.

One sidenote, I’ve been making use of GitHub’s CoPilot for small tasks lately. For example, I knew I had a small issue with cd .. inside archives and assigned that issue to copilot.

I still need to pull and manually validate the change, but I’ve found it to be incredibly useful for easy management of focused tasks.

Key commits from this phase:

  • Rename 🫣 - Final project naming
  • chore: release v0.1.0 - First release
  • Fix cd .. from archive root - Post-release fix (the Copilot PR mentioned!)

Would I Do This Again?

Absolutely. For tools like this - weekend projects, internal utilities, one-off explorers, when you know exactly what you want - this approach is perfect. I do wish I was more familiar with Rust, but I do think the combination of Rust CLIs with Claude is extremely powerful.

Tips if you try this:

  • Be specific in your initial prompt (the time spent here pays off 10x)
  • Test frequently and give feedback (don’t let Claude go too far down wrong paths)
  • Use separate sessions for bug fixes (keeps the main thread focused)
  • Trust the compiler (if it builds, it probably works)
  • Keep a plan file (seriously, learn from my mistake)

btw…I found those backups. Isn’t this site so 2002?! Maybe I should have left it archived. 😅
